offense_class: Misdemeanor (first/second); Felony (third within 10 years or two excessive BAC within 5 years)
penalty_max: 6 months (first); 1 year (second or excessive BAC first); 5 years (felony DUI)
elements: Defendant drove or was in actual physical control of a motor vehicle
On a highway, street, bridge, or public/private property open to the public
While under the influence of alcohol, drugs, or other intoxicating substances
Or while having a BAC of .08 or higher
mandatory_minimum: None (first offense, BAC under .20); 10 days if BAC .20+ (first); 30 days (third offense felony)
enhancements: Excessive BAC (.20 or higher): mandatory minimum 10 days, up to 1 year, $2,000 fine — I.C. § 18-8004C
Two excessive BAC DUIs within 5 years: automatic felony — I.C. § 18-8004C
Third offense within 10 years: felony — I.C. § 18-8005(6)
Minor under 16 in vehicle: additional penalties
Injury to another: felony — I.C. § 18-8006
notes: Idaho uses implied consent under I.C. § 18-8002. Administrative license suspension (ALS) is separate from criminal penalties. First 30 days of suspension are absolute; restricted permit with ignition interlock available after. Idaho has no per se drug limit — impairment must be proven.

statute_title: Driving Under the Influence — First Offense
elements: Defendant drove or was in actual physical control of a motor vehicle
On a highway or other place open to the public
While under the influence of alcohol, drugs, or intoxicating substances OR with a BAC of .08 or higher
No prior DUI convictions within 10 years
mandatory_minimum: None (standard first offense); 10 days if BAC .20 or higher (first 48 hours consecutive)
enhancements: BAC .20 or higher (excessive): up to 1 year jail, $2,000 fine — I.C. § 18-8004C
Minor under 16 in vehicle
notes: License suspension 90-210 days. First 30 days absolute, then restricted driving privileges with ignition interlock device available. Substance abuse evaluation required.

statute_title: Driving Under the Influence — Second Offense
elements: Defendant drove or was in actual physical control of a motor vehicle while under the influence
One prior DUI conviction within 10 years
enhancements: Two excessive BAC (.20+) DUIs within 5 years: automatic felony — I.C. § 18-8004C
BAC .20 or higher: enhanced penalties
notes: License suspension minimum 1 year. Ignition interlock device required upon reinstatement. Mandatory substance abuse treatment program.

statute_title: Driving Under the Influence — Third or Subsequent Offense (Felony)
elements: Defendant drove or was in actual physical control of a motor vehicle while under the influence
Two or more prior DUI convictions within 10 years
enhancements: Additional prior convictions: enhanced sentencing
Injury to another: separate felony under I.C. § 18-8006
notes: License suspension minimum 1 year, up to 5 years. Felony DUI triggers mandatory ignition interlock for life upon license reinstatement. Court may order substance abuse treatment.

statute_title: Driving Under the Influence — Repeat Offense
elements: Defendant drove or was in actual physical control of a motor vehicle while under the influence
One or more prior DUI convictions within 10 years
enhancements: Third offense within 10 years: felony — I.C. § 18-8005(6)
Two excessive BAC (.20+) within 5 years: felony — I.C. § 18-8004C
Injury to another: additional felony charge
notes: Idaho counts prior DUI convictions within a 10-year lookback period. License suspension escalates with each conviction. Ignition interlock required on reinstatement for repeat offenders.

offense_class: Misdemeanor (first offense); escalates same as alcohol DUI for repeat offenses
penalty_max: 6 months (first); same escalation as alcohol DUI on subsequent offenses
elements: Defendant drove or was in actual physical control of a motor vehicle
While under the influence of drugs or other intoxicating substances
Influence impaired defendant's ability to drive safely
enhancements: Multiple substances combined
Prescription drugs taken outside prescribed manner
Prior DUI conviction of any type
notes: Idaho has no per se drug impairment limit. Prosecution must prove impairment through officer testimony, Drug Recognition Expert (DRE) evaluation, or toxicology results. Blood or urine testing used instead of breath test.

elements: Defendant drove or was in actual physical control of a motor vehicle while under the influence
Defendant caused great bodily harm, permanent disability, or permanent disfigurement to another person
enhancements: Death resulting from DUI: vehicular manslaughter — I.C. § 18-4006(3)
Prior DUI convictions
notes: Aggravated DUI carries its own penalty separate from the underlying DUI charge. License suspension minimum 1 year, up to 5 years. Restitution to victims commonly ordered.

offense_class: Misdemeanor (DUI) plus potential Misdemeanor or Felony (injury to child)
penalty_max: 6 months (DUI) plus up to 10 years (injury to child if applicable)
elements: Defendant drove or was in actual physical control of a motor vehicle while under the influence
A minor under 16 was present in the vehicle
enhancements: Injury to child: felony under I.C. § 18-1501
Prior DUI convictions
notes: Idaho does not have a standalone DUI-with-minor enhancement statute. The child's presence may result in additional charges under I.C. § 18-1501 (injury to children) if circumstances likely to produce great bodily harm or death. Prosecutors frequently file both DUI and child endangerment charges.

elements: Defendant drove or was in actual physical control of a vehicle
On a highway or public property open to the public
In a manner that was careless and heedless or without due caution
At a speed or in a manner likely to endanger any person or property
enhancements: Second or subsequent offense within 5 years: 1 year/$2,000
License suspension under I.C. § 49-326
notes: Reckless driving is in Title 49 (Motor Vehicles) rather than Title 18 (Crimes). Commonly used as a plea-down from DUI. License suspension is mandatory.

statute_title: Leaving the Scene of an Accident
offense_class: Misdemeanor (property damage only); Felony (injury or death)
elements: Defendant was the driver of a vehicle involved in an accident
Accident resulted in damage to property, injury, or death
Defendant failed to stop at or near the scene
Defendant failed to provide required information or render aid
enhancements: Accident involving injury or death: felony
License revocation 1 year minimum for injury/death accident
notes: Driver must stop, provide name/address/license/registration/insurance, and render reasonable assistance to injured persons. License revocation for injury or death accident precludes any work permit or limited driving privileges.

statute_title: Leaving the Scene of an Accident Involving Injury or Death
elements: Defendant was the driver of a vehicle involved in an accident
Accident resulted in bodily injury or death to another person
Defendant failed to stop and render aid or provide information
enhancements: Death resulting: potential additional homicide charges
notes: License revocation minimum 1 year. No work permit or limited driving privileges allowed during revocation period.

elements: Defendant operated a motor vehicle
Operation of the vehicle was a significant cause contributing to the death of another person
Death occurred because of the commission of an unlawful act not amounting to a felony
Defendant acted with gross negligence
enhancements: DUI involvement: separate felony DUI charge — I.C. § 18-8004
Prior DUI convictions
notes: Idaho distinguishes vehicular manslaughter (I.C. § 18-4006(3)) from voluntary and involuntary manslaughter. The unlawful act must not amount to a felony, and gross negligence in operating the vehicle must be shown.

elements: Defendant operated a motor vehicle
Operation was a significant cause contributing to death
Death resulted from commission of an unlawful act with gross negligence
enhancements: DUI involvement: potential murder charges under depraved mind theory
Prior DUI convictions: may elevate to second-degree murder
notes: Idaho does not have a separate 'vehicular homicide' statute. Deaths caused by vehicle are charged as vehicular manslaughter under I.C. § 18-4006(3), or as murder/manslaughter under standard homicide statutes depending on mental state. DUI-related deaths may be charged as second-degree murder.

elements: Defendant drove or was in actual physical control of a motor vehicle
On Idaho highways
With knowledge that driver's license, driving privileges, or permit to drive was revoked, disqualified, or suspended
enhancements: Second offense: mandatory 2 days jail — I.C. § 18-8001(3)
Third or more within 5 years: mandatory 10 days jail — I.C. § 18-8001(4)
notes: Idaho uses the term 'Driving Without Privileges' rather than 'Driving on Suspended License.' Knowledge of the suspension is an element of the offense. Additional license suspension of 1 year on first conviction.

statute_title: Fleeing or Attempting to Elude a Peace Officer
elements: Defendant was driving a motor vehicle
A peace officer gave a visual or audible signal to stop
Defendant willfully fled or attempted to elude the pursuing police vehicle
enhancements: Traveling 30+ mph over posted speed limit: felony
Causing damage to property or bodily injury: felony
Driving in a manner endangering persons or property: felony
Leaving the state: felony
notes: Felony eluding carries license suspension 1-3 years with absolutely no driving privileges of any kind. The signal from the peace officer may be by emergency lights or siren.

elements: Defendant operated a motor vehicle on a public highway
Defendant engaged in a race, speed contest, or drag race with another vehicle
Or defendant facilitated or aided such a contest
enhancements: Injury to another: potential felony charges
Reckless driving enhancement — I.C. § 49-1401
notes: Idaho addresses racing under general reckless driving and traffic violation statutes. No standalone racing statute exists — prosecuted under reckless driving (I.C. § 49-1401) or exhibition of speed provisions.

elements: An open container of an alcoholic beverage was present in a motor vehicle
The container was in the passenger area of the vehicle
The vehicle was on a public highway or right-of-way
notes: Idaho's open container law is found in Title 23 (Alcoholic Beverages). It is an infraction, not a criminal offense. The penalty is a fine only — no jail time or criminal record. Does not apply to passengers in certain commercial vehicles.

statute_title: Tests for Alcohol Concentration and Presence of Drugs — Implied Consent
offense_class: Civil/Administrative (first refusal); Misdemeanor (second refusal within 10 years)
penalty_max: Administrative license suspension only (first); 1 year (second refusal misdemeanor)
elements: Defendant was lawfully arrested for DUI or had reasonable grounds for testing
Officer requested defendant submit to evidentiary testing
Defendant refused to submit to testing
mandatory_minimum: 180-day license suspension (first refusal); 1-year suspension (second refusal within 10 years)
enhancements: Second refusal within 10 years: misdemeanor criminal charge
Refusal is admissible as evidence at DUI trial
notes: Idaho implied consent law under I.C. § 18-8002. First refusal is administrative only (license suspension). A second refusal within 10 years becomes a misdemeanor. Refusal to submit to testing may be used as evidence of consciousness of guilt at trial.

offense_class: Felony (Schedule I narcotics, Schedule II); Misdemeanor (non-narcotic Schedule I except LSD, Schedules III-VI)
penalty_max: 7 years (Schedule I narcotic/Schedule II); 3 years (LSD); 1 year (non-narcotic Schedule I, Schedules III-VI)
elements: Defendant possessed a controlled substance
The substance is listed in the Idaho Uniform Controlled Substances schedules
Defendant did not have a valid prescription or other lawful authority
enhancements: Possession with intent to deliver: felony with enhanced penalties — I.C. § 37-2732(a)
Proximity to school or park: enhanced penalties
Prior drug convictions
notes: Idaho classifies controlled substances into Schedules I through VI under I.C. § 37-2705 through 37-2713. Possession of Schedule I narcotics (heroin, etc.) or Schedule II substances is always a felony. Non-narcotic Schedule I (except LSD), III, IV, V, and VI possession is a misdemeanor.

offense_class: Misdemeanor (3 oz or less); Felony (more than 3 oz)
penalty_max: 1 year (3 oz or less); 5 years (more than 3 oz)
elements: Defendant possessed marijuana
Defendant did not have lawful authority for possession
mandatory_minimum: $300 mandatory minimum fine (3 oz or less, age 18+)
enhancements: More than 3 ounces: felony — I.C. § 37-2732(c)(2)
Delivery or possession with intent to deliver: felony — I.C. § 37-2732(a)
Cultivation/manufacturing: felony — I.C. § 37-2732(b)
notes: Idaho has NOT legalized recreational or medical marijuana. Marijuana is classified as a Schedule I controlled substance. Possession of 3 ounces or less is a misdemeanor with a mandatory minimum $300 fine for adults 18+. Idaho remains one of the strictest states for marijuana possession.

elements: Defendant possessed cocaine (a Schedule II controlled substance)
Defendant did not have a valid prescription or lawful authority
enhancements: Possession with intent to deliver: up to life imprisonment, $25,000 fine — I.C. § 37-2732(a)
Drug trafficking quantities: mandatory minimum sentences — I.C. § 37-2732B
notes: Cocaine is a Schedule II controlled substance in Idaho. Any amount of possession is a felony. Trafficking thresholds (28 grams+) trigger mandatory minimum sentences under the trafficking statute.

elements: Defendant possessed methamphetamine (a Schedule II controlled substance)
Defendant did not have lawful authority for possession
enhancements: Possession with intent to deliver: up to life imprisonment, $25,000 fine
Trafficking quantities (28 grams+): mandatory minimum 1 year, $10,000 fine — I.C. § 37-2732B
Manufacturing: additional felony charges — I.C. § 37-2732(b)
notes: Methamphetamine is a Schedule II controlled substance. Idaho has specific trafficking thresholds: 28g+ triggers mandatory minimums. Manufacturing meth carries additional penalties and potential environmental cleanup liability.

elements: Defendant possessed heroin (Schedule I narcotic), fentanyl (Schedule II), or other opioids
Defendant did not have a valid prescription or lawful authority
enhancements: Possession with intent to deliver: up to life imprisonment
Trafficking quantities: mandatory minimum sentences — I.C. § 37-2732B
Death resulting from distribution: potential homicide charges
notes: Heroin is a Schedule I narcotic; fentanyl and most prescription opioids are Schedule II. Any possession without a valid prescription is a felony. Idaho has seen increased fentanyl-related prosecutions with trafficking charges at lower weight thresholds.

statute_title: Possession of Prescription Drugs Without Valid Prescription
penalty_max: 1 year (Schedule III-VI misdemeanor); 7 years (Schedule II felony)
elements: Defendant possessed a prescription-controlled substance
Defendant did not have a valid prescription from a licensed practitioner
enhancements: Possession with intent to distribute
Obtaining by fraud: additional charges under I.C. § 37-2734(a)
notes: Classification depends on the drug schedule. Schedule II drugs (oxycodone, hydrocodone, etc.) are felonies. Schedule III-VI drugs are misdemeanors. Prescription fraud is a separate offense under I.C. § 37-2734.

elements: Defendant knowingly possessed, delivered, manufactured, or brought into the state
A controlled substance in a quantity meeting or exceeding trafficking thresholds
mandatory_minimum: 1 year and $10,000 fine (lowest threshold); escalates with quantity
enhancements: Higher quantities: escalating mandatory minimums
Marijuana 25+ lbs: 5 years mandatory, $50,000 fine
Cocaine/meth 200+ grams: 10 years mandatory, $50,000 fine
Heroin 7+ grams: 10 years mandatory, $50,000 fine
notes: Idaho has some of the harshest drug trafficking mandatory minimums in the nation. Trafficking thresholds: marijuana (1 lb+), cocaine/meth (28g+), heroin (2g+). Judge cannot impose less than mandatory minimum. No parole eligibility during mandatory minimum period.

statute_title: Delivery or Distribution of a Controlled Substance
penalty_max: Life imprisonment (Schedule I narcotic/Schedule II); 5 years (non-narcotic Schedule I, Schedule III)
fine_max: $25,000 (Schedule I narcotic/Schedule II); $15,000 (non-narcotic Schedule I, Schedule III)
elements: Defendant delivered or distributed a controlled substance
Or possessed a controlled substance with intent to deliver
Delivery was not authorized by a valid prescription or lawful purpose
enhancements: Delivery to a minor: enhanced penalties
Within 1,000 feet of school: enhanced penalties
Trafficking quantities: mandatory minimums under I.C. § 37-2732B
notes: Delivery of Schedule I narcotics or Schedule II substances carries a maximum of life imprisonment. The statute covers sale, delivery, and possession with intent to deliver.

penalty_max: Life imprisonment (Schedule I narcotic/Schedule II); 5 years (non-narcotic Schedule I, Schedule III)
fine_max: $25,000 (Schedule I narcotic/Schedule II); $15,000 (non-narcotic Schedule I, Schedule III)
elements: Defendant manufactured, compounded, converted, produced, or processed a controlled substance
Manufacturing was not authorized by law
enhancements: Meth lab endangering children: additional charges under I.C. § 37-2737A
Environmental contamination: cleanup liability
Trafficking quantities: mandatory minimums
notes: Manufacturing methamphetamine is heavily prosecuted in Idaho. Clandestine lab operations carry additional charges for child endangerment if minors are present and environmental cleanup costs.

elements: Defendant used or possessed with intent to use drug paraphernalia
Paraphernalia was intended to plant, propagate, cultivate, grow, manufacture, prepare, test, analyze, inject, ingest, inhale, or introduce a controlled substance into the body
enhancements: Delivery of paraphernalia: up to 9 years, $30,000 fine
Delivery of paraphernalia to a minor (3+ years younger): felony up to 9 years, $30,000 fine
notes: Possession of paraphernalia is a misdemeanor, but delivery/sale of paraphernalia is a felony. Common paraphernalia includes pipes, bongs, syringes (when used for drug purposes), and rolling papers.

elements: Defendant obtained or attempted to obtain a controlled substance by fraud, deceit, misrepresentation, or subterfuge
Or defendant used a false name or gave false address in obtaining a prescription
enhancements: Multiple prescriptions from different providers ('doctor shopping')
Forging a prescription: additional forgery charges
notes: Covers prescription fraud, doctor shopping, and obtaining controlled substances through misrepresentation. Separate from general fraud statutes.

statute_title: Possession With Intent to Deliver a Controlled Substance
penalty_max: Life imprisonment (Schedule I narcotic/Schedule II); 5 years (non-narcotic Schedule I, Schedule III)
fine_max: $25,000 (Schedule I narcotic/Schedule II); $15,000 (non-narcotic Schedule I, Schedule III)
elements: Defendant possessed a controlled substance
Defendant intended to deliver or distribute the substance
Intent may be inferred from quantity, packaging, scales, cash, or other indicia
enhancements: Delivery to a minor
Within 1,000 feet of school
Trafficking quantities trigger mandatory minimums
notes: Intent to deliver is typically inferred from circumstantial evidence: quantity exceeding personal use, packaging materials, scales, large amounts of cash, multiple phones, pay/owe sheets. Same penalty structure as delivery/distribution.

penalty_max: Same as the underlying drug offense
fine_max: Same as the underlying drug offense
elements: Defendant agreed with one or more persons to commit a drug offense
At least one overt act was committed in furtherance of the conspiracy
enhancements: Conspiracy to traffic: subject to trafficking mandatory minimums
Multiple co-conspirators: potential RICO charges
notes: Idaho's conspiracy statute (I.C. § 18-1701) applies to drug offenses. Penalties mirror the underlying substantive drug offense. All members of a conspiracy are liable for foreseeable acts of co-conspirators.

elements: Defendant unlawfully killed a human being
With malice aforethought
The killing was willful, deliberate, and premeditated
Or perpetrated by means of poison, lying in wait, or torture
mandatory_minimum: Fixed term of not less than 10 years
enhancements: Killing of a peace officer, judicial officer, firefighter, or prosecutor: automatic first degree — I.C. § 18-4003(b)
Felony murder: killing during commission of arson, rape, robbery, burglary, kidnapping, or mayhem — I.C. § 18-4003(d)
Death penalty aggravators under I.C. § 19-2515
notes: Idaho retains the death penalty. First-degree murder includes premeditated killing, felony murder (during enumerated felonies), and killing of certain officials. Prosecution must prove premeditation, which can be formed in an instant. Felony murder does not require intent to kill.

elements: Defendant unlawfully killed a human being
With malice aforethought
The killing was not premeditated or deliberate (or does not qualify as first degree)
mandatory_minimum: Fixed term of not less than 10 years
enhancements: Use of a firearm during commission
Prior violent felony convictions
notes: All murder that is not first degree is second degree in Idaho. Second-degree murder requires malice (express or implied) but not premeditation. Commonly charged in cases involving extreme recklessness or depraved indifference to human life. Includes DUI deaths where defendant had prior DUI convictions.

elements: Defendant unlawfully killed a human being
Without malice
Upon a sudden quarrel or heat of passion
There was legally adequate provocation
enhancements: Use of a deadly weapon
Prior violent felony convictions
notes: Voluntary manslaughter is the intentional killing without malice, typically in the heat of passion after adequate provocation. The provocation must be such that a reasonable person would have been provoked. Cooling-off period negates the heat-of-passion defense.

elements: Defendant unlawfully killed a human being
Without malice
During the perpetration of an unlawful act not amounting to a felony
Or in the commission of a lawful act without due caution and circumspection
Or in reckless, careless, or negligent operation of a firearm or deadly weapon
enhancements: Use of a firearm or deadly weapon
Reckless conduct in the presence of others
notes: Involuntary manslaughter covers unintentional killings resulting from criminal negligence or during commission of a non-felony unlawful act. Distinguished from vehicular manslaughter (I.C. § 18-4006(3)) when a motor vehicle is the instrumentality.

penalty_max: Life imprisonment (attempted first degree); 15 years (attempted second degree)
elements: Defendant intended to kill another person
Defendant took a direct but ineffectual act toward committing murder
The act went beyond mere preparation
enhancements: Use of a deadly weapon
Attempted murder of a law enforcement officer
notes: Under I.C. § 18-306, attempted first-degree murder carries a maximum of life imprisonment. Attempted second-degree murder is punishable by up to 15 years. Specific intent to kill must be proven for attempted murder — recklessness is insufficient.

elements: Defendant committed an assault
With a deadly weapon or instrument without intent to kill
Or by any means or force likely to produce great bodily harm
enhancements: Assault on certain persons (officers, teachers, health workers): enhanced penalties — I.C. § 18-915
Use of a firearm
Gang-related: enhancement under I.C. § 18-8502
notes: Aggravated assault includes assault with a deadly weapon (even if unloaded or defective), assault by means likely to produce great bodily harm, or assault with vitriol, corrosive acid, or caustic chemical. Distinguished from simple assault (misdemeanor under I.C. § 18-901).

elements: Defendant committed an unlawful attempt, coupled with apparent ability, to commit a violent injury on the person of another

Or defendant committed an intentional, unlawful threat by word or act to do violence to the person of another, coupled with an apparent ability to carry out the threat, creating a well-founded fear in the other person
enhancements: Assault on certain persons (officers, teachers, health workers): felony under I.C. § 18-915
Use of a deadly weapon: aggravated assault — I.C. § 18-905
notes: Simple assault in Idaho is a misdemeanor punishable by up to 3 months in jail. Idaho defines assault (I.C. § 18-901) separately from battery (I.C. § 18-903). No physical contact is required — only the threat or attempt with apparent ability.

penalty_max: 6 months; 1 year if victim is pregnant and defendant knew
elements: Defendant willfully and unlawfully used force or violence upon the person of another
Or actually, intentionally, and unlawfully touched or struck another person against their will
Or unlawfully and intentionally caused bodily harm to another
enhancements: Victim is pregnant and defendant knew: up to 1 year jail
Battery on certain persons: felony — I.C. § 18-915
Aggravating circumstances: aggravated battery — I.C. § 18-907
notes: Battery is the actual physical contact; assault is the threat or attempt. Battery on a known pregnant victim doubles the maximum jail time to 1 year. Battery on officers, teachers, or health workers is a felony under I.C. § 18-915.

elements: Defendant committed a battery
And caused great bodily harm, permanent disability, or permanent disfigurement
Or used a deadly weapon or instrument
Or used any vitriol, corrosive acid, or caustic chemical
Or committed battery by means of poison or other noxious or destructive substance
enhancements: Use of a firearm: additional enhancement
Gang-related: enhancement under I.C. § 18-8502
Battery on certain protected persons: enhanced penalties
notes: Aggravated battery under I.C. § 18-907 is punishable by up to 15 years in state prison. No fine specified in the statute — the general felony fine of up to $50,000 may apply. Great bodily harm means serious physical injury.

elements: Defendant committed an assault
With a deadly weapon or instrument, including any firearm (even if unloaded or defective)
Without intent to kill
enhancements: Intent to kill: attempted murder charges instead
Victim is a law enforcement officer: enhanced under I.C. § 18-915
notes: Assault with a deadly weapon is covered under the aggravated assault statute (I.C. § 18-905). A 'deadly weapon' includes any firearm, even if unloaded or so defective it cannot be fired. If intent to kill is present, the charge escalates to attempted murder.

elements: Defendant committed an assault using a firearm
The firearm need not be loaded or functional
Without intent to kill
enhancements: Discharge of the firearm: potential additional charges
Victim is a law enforcement officer: I.C. § 18-915
Intent to kill: attempted murder
notes: Covered under the general aggravated assault statute I.C. § 18-905. Idaho specifically includes firearms — even unloaded or defective — as deadly weapons in the aggravated assault definition.

statute_title: Assault or Battery Upon Certain Personnel
elements: Defendant committed an assault or battery
Upon a law enforcement officer, firefighter, emergency medical personnel, school employee, judge, prosecutor, or other protected person
The victim was acting in the lawful discharge of official duties
Defendant knew or should have known the victim was such a person
enhancements: Use of a deadly weapon: additional charges under I.C. § 18-905 or 18-907
Causing great bodily harm: aggravated battery
notes: Idaho has a specific statute (I.C. § 18-915) elevating assault or battery on protected personnel to a felony. Protected persons include law enforcement, firefighters, EMTs, school employees, judges, and prosecutors.

elements: Defendant feloniously took personal property
Property was in the possession of another person
Property was taken from the person or immediate presence of another
Against the will of the victim
Accomplished by means of force or fear
enhancements: Use of a deadly weapon: armed robbery potential
Use of a firearm: sentencing enhancement
Great bodily injury to victim
notes: Robbery in Idaho carries a minimum of 5 years to life imprisonment under I.C. § 18-6503. Idaho does not have a separate 'armed robbery' statute — use of a weapon is a sentencing factor. The 'fear' element includes fear of injury to the person, their property, or anyone in their company.

elements: Defendant committed robbery as defined in I.C. § 18-6501
Defendant was armed with a deadly weapon during the commission of the robbery
enhancements: Firearm enhancement
Great bodily injury to victim
Multiple victims
notes: Idaho does not have a separate armed robbery statute. Armed robbery is charged under the general robbery statute (I.C. § 18-6501) with weapon use as an aggravating factor at sentencing. The penalty range (5 years to life) is the same as unarmed robbery, but judges typically impose higher sentences when weapons are involved.

penalty_max: Death or life imprisonment (first degree); 25 years (second degree)
elements: Defendant willfully seized, confined, inveigled, decoyed, kidnapped, abducted, or carried away another person
By any means whatsoever
With intent to cause the victim to be confined or imprisoned against their will
For first degree: with intent to obtain ransom, extort, commit robbery, commit lewd acts, inflict bodily harm, or facilitate a felony
enhancements: Kidnapping a child under 16: first-degree kidnapping
Kidnapping for ransom or extortion: first-degree
Rape or sexual assault during kidnapping: first-degree
notes: Idaho distinguishes first-degree kidnapping (I.C. § 18-4502, punishable by death or life) from second-degree kidnapping (I.C. § 18-4503, punishable by 1-25 years). First-degree involves specific aggravating intents. Parental kidnapping has separate provisions.

elements: Defendant unlawfully violated the personal liberty of another
enhancements: If force or threat used: potential felony charges
If victim is a minor: enhanced penalties
notes: Idaho uses the term 'false imprisonment' (I.C. § 18-2901) rather than 'unlawful imprisonment.' It is generally a misdemeanor but can escalate depending on circumstances. Distinguished from kidnapping by the absence of movement or specific criminal intent.

elements: Defendant took a motor vehicle from the person or immediate presence of the victim
By means of force or fear
Against the will of the victim
enhancements: Use of a firearm or deadly weapon
Great bodily injury to victim
Multiple victims
notes: Idaho does not have a standalone carjacking statute. Vehicle takings by force are prosecuted as robbery under I.C. § 18-6501 with the same penalty range of 5 years to life.

penalty_max: 25 years (first degree); 15 years (second degree); 10 years (third degree)
elements: Defendant willfully and unlawfully set fire to or burned, or caused to be burned
Any structure, forest land, or property
First degree: occupied structure or causing bodily harm
Second degree: unoccupied structure
Third degree: personal property valued over $1,000
enhancements: First degree (occupied structure or bodily injury): up to 25 years, $100,000 — I.C. § 18-805
Arson resulting in death: potential murder charges under felony murder rule
Insurance fraud motivation: additional charges
notes: Idaho has three degrees of arson. First degree involves occupied structures or bodily harm. Second degree involves unoccupied structures. Third degree involves personal property over $1,000. Arson is an enumerated felony for felony murder purposes.

elements: Defendant entered an occupied dwelling
With intent to commit theft or any felony therein
enhancements: Use of a deadly weapon: additional charges
Assault or battery during entry: aggravated charges
Victim present: aggravating factor at sentencing
notes: Idaho does not have a separate home invasion statute. Burglary of an occupied dwelling is prosecuted under the general burglary statute (I.C. § 18-1401). Entry of an inhabited dwelling is an aggravating factor considered at sentencing.

elements: Defendant obtained property of another by threatening to inflict bodily injury, accuse of crime, expose secrets, take or withhold official action, or bring about a strike
The threat compelled the victim to surrender property
enhancements: Threats involving violence: potential additional charges
Public official involvement: enhanced penalties
notes: Idaho treats extortion as a form of theft under I.C. § 18-2403(2)(e). If the property value exceeds $1,000, it is grand theft (felony). Blackmail and extortion are prosecuted under the theft statutes rather than a standalone extortion law.

offense_class: Misdemeanor (simple threat); Felony (aggravated or with deadly weapon)
elements: Defendant made an intentional, unlawful threat by word or act to do violence
Defendant had apparent ability to carry out the threat
The threat created a well-founded fear in the victim
enhancements: Use of a deadly weapon: aggravated assault — I.C. § 18-905
Threat directed at school, government building, or public gathering: potential federal charges
notes: Idaho does not have a standalone 'terroristic threats' statute. Threats are prosecuted under assault (I.C. § 18-901), aggravated assault (I.C. § 18-905), or telephone harassment statutes. Bomb threats are prosecuted under I.C. § 18-3302.

elements: Defendant wrongfully took, obtained, or withheld property from an owner
With intent to deprive the owner of the property
Or with intent to appropriate the property to themselves or a third person
enhancements: Value over $1,000: grand theft (felony) — I.C. § 18-2407
Theft of a firearm: grand theft regardless of value
Theft from the person: grand theft regardless of value
Theft of livestock: grand theft regardless of value
notes: Idaho's felony theft threshold is $1,000 — one of the lowest in the nation. Grand theft is also triggered regardless of value for certain property types: firearms, livestock taken from the range, property taken from the person, and public records. Idaho consolidated theft statutes under I.C. § 18-2403.

elements: Defendant committed theft as defined in I.C. § 18-2403
Value of property taken exceeds $1,000
Or the property is a firearm, livestock from the range, or was taken from the person of another
enhancements: Theft of a motor vehicle: separate charge under I.C. § 49-228
Pattern of theft activity: organized retail theft
notes: Grand theft threshold in Idaho is $1,000. Felony punishable by 1-14 years in state prison and/or up to $5,000 fine. Certain property types (firearms, livestock, property from the person, public records) qualify as grand theft regardless of value.

elements: Defendant committed theft as defined in I.C. § 18-2403
Value of property taken is under $1,000
Property does not fall into grand theft categories
enhancements: Second petit theft conviction: potential enhanced misdemeanor
Value approaching $1,000: close to felony threshold
notes: Idaho uses the term 'petit theft' (not 'petty theft'). Misdemeanor punishable by up to 1 year in county jail and/or $1,000 fine. The $1,000 threshold is one of the lowest felony thresholds in the United States.

statute_title: Shoplifting — Taken or Converted Merchandise as Theft
elements: Defendant altered, transferred, or removed a label, price tag, or marking on merchandise
From a retail mercantile establishment
With intent to purchase at less than retail price
Or defendant concealed merchandise with intent to deprive the merchant
enhancements: Value over $1,000: grand theft (felony)
Organized retail theft: enhanced penalties
Use of device to defeat anti-theft measures
notes: Shoplifting in Idaho is covered by I.C. § 18-4624 (price tag alteration) and prosecuted as theft under the general theft statute. Civil liability to the merchant is also available under I.C. § 48-703 (up to $300 or 3x damages).

elements: Defendant committed theft from a retail establishment
By price tag switching, concealment, or fraudulent return
enhancements: Organized scheme involving multiple thefts
Value aggregation over multiple incidents
notes: Idaho prosecutes retail fraud under general theft and shoplifting statutes. No standalone organized retail theft statute exists, but aggregate value across incidents can elevate charges to grand theft.

elements: Defendant entered a house, room, apartment, tenement, store, shop, warehouse, mill, barn, stable, outhouse, building, tent, vessel, vehicle, trailer, airplane, or railroad car
With intent to commit theft or any felony
enhancements: Occupied dwelling: aggravating factor at sentencing
Nighttime entry: considered aggravating
Armed during entry: additional weapons charges
notes: Idaho has a single burglary statute (I.C. § 18-1401) — no degree system. Punishable by 1-10 years under I.C. § 18-1403. Intent must exist at the time of entry. Unlike many states, Idaho burglary covers virtually any structure, including vehicles and railroad cars.

elements: Defendant entered a house, room, or apartment
With intent to commit theft or any felony
enhancements: Occupied at the time: aggravating sentencing factor
Violence during entry: additional assault/battery charges
notes: Idaho does not distinguish residential from commercial burglary in statute — both fall under I.C. § 18-1401 with the same 1-10 year penalty range. However, residential burglary is treated as more serious at sentencing and is an enumerated felony under the felony murder rule.

elements: Defendant entered a store, shop, warehouse, mill, or commercial building
With intent to commit theft or any felony
enhancements: After-hours entry: commonly charged factor
Security system bypass: evidence of premeditation
notes: Same statute and penalty range as residential burglary (I.C. § 18-1401). Commercial burglary typically involves entry into closed businesses with intent to steal. Idaho does not have a 'shoplifting by entry' statute — unlawful entry with intent to steal from a store is burglary.

elements: Defendant wrongfully took or withheld a motor vehicle from the owner
With intent to deprive the owner of the vehicle
Or with intent to temporarily appropriate the vehicle
enhancements: Multiple vehicle thefts: pattern of criminal activity
Theft for use in another crime: additional charges
notes: Motor vehicle theft is prosecuted as grand theft under I.C. § 18-2407 since vehicles typically exceed the $1,000 threshold. Idaho also has I.C. § 49-228 covering vehicle registration fraud. Joyriding may be charged as a lesser offense.

elements: Defendant received, retained, or disposed of property of another
Knowing that the property had been stolen
With intent to deprive the owner thereof
enhancements: Value over $1,000: grand theft (felony)
Dealing in stolen property as business
notes: Idaho treats receiving stolen property as a form of theft under I.C. § 18-2403(4). Same penalty structure as other theft — petit (misdemeanor) or grand (felony) based on value or property type.

elements: Defendant maliciously injured or destroyed real or personal property of another
enhancements: Damage over $1,000: felony
Damage to public property or infrastructure: potential enhanced penalties
Hate crime motivation: enhancement under I.C. § 18-7902
notes: Idaho uses 'malicious injury to property' rather than 'vandalism' or 'criminal mischief.' The $1,000 damage threshold determines felony versus misdemeanor. Restitution is commonly ordered. Graffiti offenses are included.

elements: Defendant maliciously injured or destroyed property belonging to another
enhancements: Damage exceeding $1,000: felony — I.C. § 18-7001
Damage to critical infrastructure
notes: Idaho does not have a separate 'criminal mischief' statute. Property destruction is charged under I.C. § 18-7001 (malicious injury to property). Same statute as vandalism.

elements: Defendant entered the real property of another
After being forbidden to enter by the owner or authorized agent
Or remained on the property after being asked to leave
enhancements: Trespass with intent to commit a crime: burglary charges
Repeat trespass after warning
notes: Idaho's trespass statute (I.C. § 18-7008) covers various forms of unlawful entry including entering posted land, entering after being forbidden, and remaining after being told to leave. Trespass on railroad property, agricultural land, and mining claims have specific provisions.

penalty_max: 6 months (first misdemeanor); 1 year (second misdemeanor); 10 years (felony with traumatic injury)
elements: Defendant committed an assault or battery
Against a household member
Household member includes spouse, former spouse, person cohabiting, or person with a child in common
enhancements: Traumatic injury: felony, up to 10 years — I.C. § 18-918(2)
Prior domestic violence conviction: enhanced misdemeanor penalties
In the presence of a child: maximum penalties doubled — I.C. § 18-918(4)
Attempted strangulation: separate felony up to 15 years — I.C. § 18-923
notes: Idaho's domestic violence statute (I.C. § 18-918) covers both assault and battery against household members. Traumatic injury elevates to felony. Penalties are doubled when committed in the presence of a child under 16. Attempted strangulation is a separate, more serious felony.

penalty_max: 6 months (first); 1 year (prior conviction); 10 years (traumatic injury felony)
elements: Defendant committed a battery (willful and unlawful use of force or violence)
Against a household member
Battery did not result in traumatic injury (misdemeanor) OR resulted in traumatic injury (felony)
enhancements: Prior domestic violence conviction: enhanced penalty — I.C. § 18-918(3)(b)
Traumatic injury: felony — I.C. § 18-918(2)
In the presence of a child: penalties doubled
Attempted strangulation: I.C. § 18-923
notes: Domestic battery without traumatic injury is a misdemeanor. With a prior conviction, the maximum increases to 1 year and $2,000 fine. Traumatic injury elevates to felony with up to 10 years. Idaho mandates a domestic violence evaluation for all convictions.

elements: Defendant willfully caused or permitted a child to suffer
Or inflicted unjustifiable physical pain or mental suffering on a child
Under circumstances or conditions likely to produce great bodily harm or death
enhancements: Death of a child: potential murder charges
Pattern of abuse: aggravating factor
Child under 12: aggravating factor at sentencing
notes: Idaho uses 'Injury to Children' (I.C. § 18-1501) rather than 'child abuse.' The statute has both misdemeanor and felony provisions. Felony applies when circumstances are likely to produce great bodily harm or death. Mandatory reporting requirements apply to professionals.

offense_class: Misdemeanor (circumstances not likely to produce great harm); Felony (circumstances likely to produce great bodily harm or death)
elements: Defendant had care or custody of a child
Defendant willfully caused or permitted the child to be placed in a situation that endangered the child's person or health
enhancements: DUI with child in vehicle: concurrent I.C. § 18-8004 charges
Drug exposure: additional charges if drugs present
Bodily injury or death resulting: felony
notes: Child endangerment is prosecuted under the same statute as child abuse (I.C. § 18-1501). The misdemeanor version covers situations not likely to produce great harm. The felony version covers situations likely to produce great bodily harm or death.

offense_class: Misdemeanor (no great harm likely); Felony (great bodily harm or death likely)
elements: Defendant had care or custody of a child
Defendant willfully caused or permitted the person or health of the child to be injured
Or willfully caused or permitted the child to be placed in an endangering situation
enhancements: Death resulting from neglect: potential manslaughter or murder charges
Pattern of neglect: aggravating factor
notes: Child neglect is prosecuted under I.C. § 18-1501 (Injury to Children). Idaho does not have a separate neglect statute. Includes failure to provide necessary food, clothing, shelter, medical care, or supervision.

elements: A protection order was issued against the defendant
Defendant had notice of the order
Defendant violated a term or condition of the order
enhancements: Second violation: enhanced penalties
Violation involving assault or battery: additional criminal charges
Violation while on probation: probation revocation
notes: Protection order violations are under I.C. § 39-6312 (Title 39 Health and Safety, not Title 18 Crimes). First violation is a misdemeanor. Contact or no-contact order violations may also be prosecuted under I.C. § 18-920.

elements: Defendant knowingly and maliciously engaged in a course of conduct
That seriously alarmed, annoyed, or harassed the victim
Such as would cause a reasonable person substantial emotional distress
Or such as would cause a reasonable person to fear death or physical injury
enhancements: Aggravating factors elevate to first-degree stalking (felony) — I.C. § 18-7905
Prior stalking conviction within 7 years: first-degree stalking
notes: Idaho has two degrees of stalking. Second degree (I.C. § 18-7906) is a misdemeanor. 'Course of conduct' means repeated acts of nonconsensual contact. Single incidents generally do not constitute stalking.

elements: Defendant committed stalking in the second degree (I.C. § 18-7906)

Plus one or more aggravating factors: violation of a protective/no-contact order, violation of probation/parole, victim under 16, possession of a deadly weapon, or prior stalking conviction within 7 years
enhancements: Repeat first-degree stalking within 7 years: enhanced sentencing
Stalking combined with other offenses (assault, threats)
notes: First-degree stalking under I.C. § 18-7905 is a felony requiring the base stalking conduct plus an aggravating factor. A prior conviction for either degree of stalking within 7 years automatically elevates a new stalking charge to first degree.

offense_class: Misdemeanor (second degree); Felony (first degree with aggravating factors)
elements: Defendant used electronic communications to knowingly and maliciously engage in a course of conduct
That seriously alarmed, annoyed, or harassed the victim
Such as would cause a reasonable person substantial emotional distress
enhancements: Aggravating factors: elevates to first-degree stalking
Threats of death or bodily injury via electronic means
notes: Idaho prosecutes cyberstalking under the general stalking statutes (I.C. § 18-7905 and 18-7906). I.C. § 18-7907 specifically addresses use of telephone or electronic communication to harass. Electronic communications are included in the definition of 'nonconsensual contact.'

statute_title: Harassment by Telephone or Electronic Communication
elements: Defendant used a telephone or electronic communication device
To annoy, terrify, threaten, intimidate, harass, or offend another person
The communication was made with intent to harass
enhancements: Threats of violence: potential felony assault charges
Repeated conduct: stalking charges — I.C. § 18-7906
notes: Idaho's harassment statute (I.C. § 18-7907) specifically addresses telephone and electronic harassment. Broader harassment patterns may be charged as stalking. In-person harassment is typically charged as disturbing the peace or assault.

statute_title: Abuse, Exploitation, or Neglect of a Vulnerable Adult
penalty_max: 10 years (felony for abuse/exploitation); 1 year (misdemeanor for neglect)
elements: Defendant committed abuse, exploitation, or neglect
Against a vulnerable adult (person 18+ who is unable to protect themselves from abuse, neglect, or exploitation due to physical or mental condition)
enhancements: Death resulting from abuse: potential homicide charges
Financial exploitation exceeding $1,000: felony
Pattern of abuse: aggravating factor
notes: Idaho uses 'Vulnerable Adult' rather than 'Elder' — covers adults of any age with qualifying physical or mental conditions, not just the elderly. Financial exploitation is a common form prosecuted under this statute. Mandatory reporting requirements apply.

statute_title: Financial Exploitation of a Vulnerable Adult
elements: Defendant exploited a vulnerable adult
Exploitation includes misuse of funds, property, or assets of a vulnerable adult
Through undue influence, coercion, manipulation, or deception
enhancements: Amount exceeding $1,000: felony
Position of trust (caregiver, fiduciary): aggravating factor
notes: Financial exploitation of vulnerable adults is prosecuted under I.C. § 18-1505. Idaho's definition of vulnerable adult covers those unable to protect themselves due to physical or mental condition, regardless of age.

elements: Defendant carried a concealed weapon on or about their person
Without being exempted under Idaho law
enhancements: Carrying in a prohibited location: additional charges — I.C. § 18-3302C
Felony conviction: separate offense under I.C. § 18-3316
notes: Idaho enacted constitutional carry in 2016 — most adults 18+ can carry concealed without a permit within city limits, and 21+ outside city limits. Restrictions remain for certain persons (felons, mentally ill, juveniles under 18) and certain locations (courthouses, schools, jails). Idaho is one of the most permissive states for firearms.

elements: Defendant has been previously convicted of a felony
Defendant purchased, owned, possessed, or had under custody or control any firearm
enhancements: Possession during commission of another felony
Federal prosecution under 18 USC 922(g)
notes: Under I.C. § 18-3316, convicted felons are prohibited from possessing firearms. Idaho has an automatic rights restoration provision — firearm rights are automatically restored 5 years after completion of sentence for most felons, unless the felony is listed in I.C. § 18-310. Violent felons and certain sex offenders are permanently prohibited.

elements: Defendant carried a concealed weapon
Defendant was not eligible under Idaho's constitutional carry provisions
Or defendant carried in a location where concealed carry is prohibited
enhancements: Prohibited person (felon, juvenile): separate felony charge
Prohibited location (courthouse, school): additional charges
notes: Idaho's 2016 constitutional carry law dramatically reduced concealed carry violations. Violations now primarily involve prohibited persons (felons, certain minors) or prohibited locations. Out-of-state residents under 21 are subject to different rules within city limits.

statute_title: Unlawful Discharge of a Firearm at a Dwelling or Occupied Building
elements: Defendant intentionally and unlawfully discharged a firearm
At an inhabited dwelling house, occupied building, occupied motor vehicle, inhabited mobile home, or inhabited camper
enhancements: Injury to any person: additional assault/battery charges
Death resulting: potential murder/manslaughter charges
notes: I.C. § 18-3317 specifically addresses discharging a firearm at occupied structures. General discharge of firearms in prohibited areas may also be addressed by local ordinances. Discharging at an occupied vehicle is included.

elements: Defendant carried a weapon in an unauthorized manner or location
Without being eligible under constitutional carry or permit
enhancements: Carrying in a school: felony under I.C. § 18-3302D
Carrying in courthouse or jail: I.C. § 18-3302C
notes: Idaho's constitutional carry significantly limits this charge. Most violations involve prohibited locations (courthouses, schools, jails) or prohibited persons. City and county governments cannot enact firearm restrictions more restrictive than state law (preemption under I.C. § 18-3302J).

statute_title: Possession of a Destructive Device or Prohibited Weapon
elements: Defendant possessed a destructive device, bomb, or prohibited weapon
Without lawful authority
enhancements: Use in commission of a crime: additional charges
Possession near schools or public buildings
notes: Idaho is generally permissive on firearms but prohibits destructive devices and certain other weapons. Short-barreled rifles and shotguns, silencers, and machine guns are legal under Idaho law if compliant with federal NFA requirements.

statute_title: Use of a Firearm During Commission of a Felony
penalty_max: Enhanced sentence added to underlying felony
elements: Defendant committed or attempted to commit a felony
Defendant displayed, used, threatened, or attempted to use a firearm or deadly weapon during the commission of the felony
enhancements: Mandatory minimum sentence enhancement under I.C. § 19-2520
Discharge of the firearm: additional enhancement
notes: I.C. § 19-2520 provides for enhanced sentences when a deadly weapon is used during a felony. Not a standalone charge but an enhancement to the underlying felony. Judge must consider the use of a weapon at sentencing.

statute_title: Carrying a Weapon in a Prohibited Place
elements: Defendant possessed a firearm or other weapon
In a courthouse, juvenile detention facility, or jail/prison
enhancements: On school grounds: felony under I.C. § 18-3302D
notes: Idaho's list of prohibited locations is very short compared to most states: courthouses, juvenile detention facilities, and jails. Schools are addressed under a separate statute. Private property owners may prohibit weapons but violation is trespass, not a weapons offense.

statute_title: Possession of a Weapon on School Property
elements: Defendant possessed a firearm or other weapon
On or about school property, a school bus, or at a school-sponsored event
Defendant was not an exempt person (school security, law enforcement, person with written permission)
enhancements: Discharge of weapon on school property: additional charges
Threatening with weapon: felony assault charges
notes: Exemptions include law enforcement, authorized security, persons with written permission from school officials, and unloaded firearms in locked vehicles on school parking lots. Enhanced concealed weapons license holders may be exempt in some circumstances.

elements: Defendant possessed, manufactured, or transported an explosive or destructive device
Without lawful authority
enhancements: Use of explosive to damage property: arson charges
Injury or death resulting: additional charges
notes: Explosives for lawful purposes (mining, construction, agriculture) require proper permits. Possession of materials with intent to manufacture an explosive device is separately criminal.

elements: Defendant illegally sold, transferred, or trafficked firearms
Without proper federal firearms license
Or sold to prohibited persons
enhancements: Sale to a prohibited person: enhanced penalties
Interstate trafficking: federal prosecution
notes: Weapons trafficking is primarily prosecuted under federal law (18 USC 922). Idaho state law addresses illegal sales but most trafficking cases are handled federally. Idaho does not have a standalone state weapons trafficking statute.

elements: Defendant obtained or recorded personal identifying information of another person
Without authorization
With intent to use or to aid another person in using the information to obtain credit, money, goods, services, or anything of value
enhancements: Multiple victims: enhanced penalties
Elderly victim: additional charges under I.C. § 18-1505
Financial loss exceeding $1,000: additional restitution
notes: Idaho's identity theft statute (I.C. § 18-3126) covers misappropriation of personal identifying information. The $50,000 fine maximum is unusually high for Idaho. Restitution to victims is mandatory.

elements: Defendant was entrusted with property of another
Defendant knowingly appropriated the property to their own use or benefit
Without consent of the owner
enhancements: Embezzlement by public officer: enhanced under I.C. § 18-5701
Amount exceeding $1,000: felony
notes: Idaho treats embezzlement as a form of theft under I.C. § 18-2403(3) rather than a standalone offense. Penalties follow the grand theft/petit theft structure based on value. Embezzlement by public officers is a separate, more serious offense.

elements: Defendant falsely made, altered, forged, or counterfeited a document
Including deeds, wills, bonds, bank notes, checks, or other financial instruments
With intent to defraud another
enhancements: Multiple forged instruments: aggregate charges
Government documents: additional charges
notes: Forgery under I.C. § 18-3601 is a felony punishable by up to 14 years. This is one of the more severely punished property crimes in Idaho. Covers a broad range of documents including commercial instruments, public records, and official documents.

elements: Defendant falsely made or counterfeited currency, instruments, or trade-marks
With intent to defraud
enhancements: Large-scale counterfeiting operation: federal prosecution
Distribution of counterfeit goods: enhanced penalties
notes: Currency counterfeiting is primarily a federal offense. Idaho's forgery statute (I.C. § 18-3601) covers counterfeiting of instruments. Counterfeiting trade-marks (I.C. § 18-3614) is a separate misdemeanor offense.

elements: Defendant issued a check
Knowing there were insufficient funds to cover the check
With intent to defraud
enhancements: Pattern of bad check writing: aggregate value
Amount exceeding $1,000: felony
notes: Bad checks under I.C. § 18-3106 follow the general theft penalty structure. The check writer has a period to make good on the check after notification before criminal prosecution proceeds. Civil remedies are also available to the payee.

elements: Defendant used a credit card, debit card, or card number
That belonged to another person or was counterfeit
With intent to obtain goods, services, or money
Or defendant used their own card knowing it was revoked or expired
enhancements: Multiple victims: aggregate charges
Use of stolen identity: additional I.C. § 18-3126 charges
Interstate fraud: federal prosecution
notes: Idaho has specific credit card crime statutes (I.C. § 18-3124 through 18-3128). Covers theft of cards, fraudulent use, counterfeiting, and possession of machinery for counterfeiting. Distinct from general fraud and identity theft statutes.

penalty_max: 14 years (if over $1,000 under theft statute); 5 years (general felony)
elements: Defendant knowingly made a false or fraudulent insurance claim
Or prepared false documentation to support a claim
With intent to defraud an insurer
enhancements: Arson to collect insurance: additional I.C. § 18-802 charges
Pattern of fraud: organized crime potential
notes: Insurance fraud may be prosecuted under general theft/fraud statutes or specific insurance code provisions. Arson committed for insurance purposes carries enhanced penalties.

elements: Defendant willfully attempted to evade or defeat any Idaho tax
Or filed a fraudulent return with intent to evade tax
enhancements: Large-scale evasion: federal prosecution under 26 USC 7201
Pattern of fraud: enhanced penalties
notes: Idaho tax fraud is prosecuted under Title 63 (Revenue and Taxation). Willful failure to file or fraudulent filing can result in felony charges. Most significant tax fraud cases are prosecuted federally.

elements: Defendant knowingly conducted a financial transaction
Involving proceeds of unlawful activity
With intent to promote the unlawful activity or conceal the nature/source of the proceeds
enhancements: Large amounts: federal prosecution under 18 USC 1956
Connection to drug trafficking: enhanced penalties
notes: Idaho's money laundering statute (I.C. § 18-8201) covers transactions involving proceeds of unlawful activity. Most significant money laundering cases are prosecuted federally. State charges typically accompany other felony prosecutions.

elements: Defendant obtained property of another by deception
Created or reinforced a false impression including false promises
With intent to deprive the owner of the property
enhancements: Elderly victim: enhanced under I.C. § 18-1505
Value over $1,000: grand theft (felony)
notes: General fraud is prosecuted as theft by deception under Idaho's consolidated theft statute (I.C. § 18-2403(2)). Covers a broad range of fraudulent schemes. Penalty depends on value of property obtained.

elements: Defendant obtained public assistance benefits
Through false statements, misrepresentation, or concealment of material facts
With intent to defraud
enhancements: Amount exceeding $1,000: felony
Pattern of fraud: aggregate amounts
notes: Welfare fraud is prosecuted under both the specific public assistance fraud statute (I.C. § 56-227) and general theft statutes. Repayment of fraudulently obtained benefits is mandatory in addition to criminal penalties.

elements: Defendant submitted false claims for healthcare services
To Medicaid, Medicare, or other healthcare programs
With intent to defraud
enhancements: Large-scale fraud: federal prosecution
Harm to patients: additional charges
notes: Healthcare fraud involving federal programs (Medicaid, Medicare) is typically prosecuted federally. Idaho state charges are brought under general fraud/theft statutes. The Idaho Attorney General's Medicaid Fraud Control Unit handles state-level investigations.

elements: Defendant knowingly accessed or attempted to access a computer, computer system, or computer network without authorization
Or exceeded authorized access
With intent to commit theft, fraud, or cause damage
enhancements: Damage exceeding $1,000: felony
Access to government systems: enhanced penalties
Interstate activity: federal prosecution under CFAA
notes: Idaho's Computer Crime Act (I.C. § 18-2201 through 18-2202) covers unauthorized access, data theft, and computer fraud. Severity depends on intent and damage caused. Federal prosecution is common for significant cases.

statute_title: Forcible Sexual Penetration by Use of Foreign Object
elements: Defendant penetrated the oral, anal, or vaginal opening of the victim
By use of a foreign object, substance, instrument, or device
Against the victim's will by force, violence, duress, menace, or threat of great bodily harm
enhancements: Victim under 16: enhanced penalties
Use of a weapon: additional charges
Repeat sex offense: registration and enhanced sentencing
notes: Idaho does not use the term 'sexual battery' or 'criminal sexual conduct.' Forcible sexual penetration with a foreign object is charged under I.C. § 18-6608. Other sexual contact offenses are covered under the lewd conduct statute (I.C. § 18-6607).

elements: Defendant accomplished penetration (however slight) of the oral, anal, or vaginal opening
Against the victim's will by force or threat of force
Or where the victim was incapable of giving consent due to mental condition or incapacity
Or where the victim was under the age of consent
enhancements: Victim under 16, perpetrator 18+: mandatory sex offender registration
Use of a weapon: additional charges
Kidnapping: first-degree kidnapping potential
notes: Idaho uses the term 'rape' (I.C. § 18-6101) rather than 'sexual assault.' Punishment is 1 year to life under I.C. § 18-6104. Idaho's rape statute covers multiple scenarios including force, incapacity, age, and position of authority.

elements: Defendant perpetrated an act of penetration (however slight) of the oral, anal, or vaginal opening with the defendant's penis
Where the victim was under 16 and defendant was 18+
Or where the victim was 16-17 and defendant was 3+ years older
Or where accomplished by force, violence, duress, menace, or threat
Or where victim was incapable of consent due to mental condition or intoxication
Or where victim was unconscious
enhancements: Defendant held position of authority over victim
Use of a deadly weapon
Victim suffered great bodily harm
notes: Idaho defines rape under I.C. § 18-6101 and punishment under I.C. § 18-6104. The sentence is not less than 1 year, up to life at the discretion of the judge. Male rape is covered. Spousal rape is recognized. Sex offender registration is mandatory.

elements: Defendant perpetrated an act of penetration
Victim was under 16 and defendant was 18 or older (subsection 1)
Or victim was 16 or 17 and defendant was 3 or more years older (subsection 2)
enhancements: Victim under 12: aggravating factor
Position of trust or authority: aggravating factor
notes: Idaho has a two-tier age-of-consent structure: under 16 (defendant must be 18+) and 16-17 (defendant must be 3+ years older). Both are felonies carrying 1 year to life. There is no Romeo-and-Juliet exception for close-in-age peers when the victim is under 16.

elements: Defendant intentionally exposed their genitals
In a public place or where others were present
Under circumstances likely to cause affront or alarm
enhancements: Exposure to a minor: potential lewd conduct charges — I.C. § 18-1508
Prior sex offense conviction: enhanced penalties
notes: Misdemeanor indecent exposure is a relatively minor offense. However, if exposure is directed at a minor under 16, it can be charged as lewd conduct with a minor (I.C. § 18-1508), which is a felony punishable by up to life imprisonment.

elements: Defendant solicited or agreed to pay for sexual conduct
Or defendant entered a house of prostitution for the purpose of engaging in sexual conduct
enhancements: Second offense: enhanced misdemeanor — 1 year
Involving a minor: felony sex trafficking charges — I.C. § 18-8602
notes: Idaho criminalizes both the buyer (patronizing, I.C. § 18-5614) and seller (prostitution, I.C. § 18-5613). Both are misdemeanors for first offense. Solicitation involving a minor triggers human trafficking charges.

elements: Defendant engaged in or offered to engage in sexual conduct
In exchange for a fee
enhancements: Second offense: enhanced misdemeanor
Promoting prostitution: felony — I.C. § 18-5608
notes: Prostitution in Idaho is a misdemeanor for the individual. Promoting, facilitating, or profiting from another's prostitution (pandering) is a felony. Human trafficking charges apply when force, fraud, or coercion is involved.

elements: Defendant procured, encouraged, or induced another person to engage in prostitution
Or defendant received money or other consideration for arranging prostitution
enhancements: Involving a minor: human trafficking under I.C. § 18-8602
Force, fraud, or coercion: human trafficking
notes: Idaho has severe penalties for pandering. I.C. § 18-5609 (procuring for purposes of prostitution) carries up to life imprisonment. I.C. § 18-5608 covers keeping a house of prostitution. These are far more serious than the prostitution offense itself.

statute_title: Sexual Exploitation of a Child by Use of Technology
elements: Defendant used the internet or electronic communication
To entice, induce, or solicit a child to engage in sexual activity
Or to distribute sexually explicit material to a child
enhancements: Actual meeting with the child: enhanced penalties
Production of child exploitation material: additional charges
Distribution across state lines: federal prosecution
notes: Idaho's online solicitation statute (I.C. § 18-1509A) covers using technology to sexually exploit minors. Separate from child pornography statutes. Undercover sting operations are common. The penalty is significant at up to 15 years.

elements: Defendant produced, distributed, or possessed sexually exploitative material
Involving a child under 18
Material depicts actual sexual conduct by the child
enhancements: Production: up to 30 years — I.C. § 18-1507(2)
Distribution: up to 10 years
Victim under 12: aggravating factor
Large collection: evidence of pattern
notes: Idaho's child exploitation statutes are severe. Production carries up to 30 years. Mandatory sex offender registration. Federal prosecution is common and carries mandatory minimums that Idaho state law does not impose.

statute_title: Possession of Sexually Exploitative Material of a Child
elements: Defendant knowingly possessed sexually exploitative material
The material depicted a child under 18 engaged in sexual conduct
Defendant knew or should have known the material depicted a minor
enhancements: Large volume of material: aggravating factor
Distribution: enhanced penalties under I.C. § 18-1507
Federal prosecution: mandatory minimums under 18 USC 2252
notes: Possession alone is a felony in Idaho carrying up to 10 years. Mandatory sex offender registration upon conviction. Many cases are referred to federal authorities for prosecution under federal mandatory minimums.

statute_title: Production of Sexually Exploitative Material of a Child
elements: Defendant produced, directed, or promoted sexually exploitative material
Involving a child under 18
Material depicts the child engaged in actual sexual conduct
enhancements: Multiple victims: separate charges per victim
Victim under 12: aggravating factor
Use of force or coercion: additional charges
notes: Production carries up to 30 years — the most severe penalty for child exploitation offenses in Idaho. Lifetime sex offender registration required. Federal charges commonly run concurrent.

statute_title: Failure to Register as a Sex Offender
elements: Defendant was required to register as a sex offender under the Idaho Sex Offender Registration Act
Defendant failed to register, update registration, or provide required information
Failure was knowing and willful
enhancements: Multiple failures to register: enhanced sentencing
Absconding from jurisdiction: additional charges
notes: Idaho's Sex Offender Registration Act (I.C. § 18-8301 et seq.) requires registration for violent sexual predators, sexual offenders, and kidnapping offenders. Failure to register, update address, or comply with registration requirements is a felony up to 10 years.

elements: Defendant recruited, harbored, transported, or obtained a person
For the purpose of sexual servitude
Through force, fraud, or coercion
enhancements: Minor victim: up to life imprisonment — I.C. § 18-8602(2)
Multiple victims: separate charges
Use of force or serious harm: aggravating factors
notes: Idaho has specific human trafficking statutes (I.C. § 18-8601 through 18-8605). Sexual trafficking of a minor does not require proof of force, fraud, or coercion — the minor's age alone is sufficient. Victims of trafficking have affirmative defenses to prostitution charges.

elements: Defendant committed non-consensual sexual contact or penetration with a foreign object
Against the victim's will by force or threat
enhancements: Victim is a minor
Use of a weapon
Prior sex offense
notes: Idaho does not have a statute specifically titled 'sexual battery.' Non-consensual sexual contact is prosecuted under rape (I.C. § 18-6101), forcible penetration by foreign object (I.C. § 18-6608), or lewd conduct statutes (I.C. § 18-6607). Terminology varies from other states.

elements: Defendant maliciously and willfully disturbed the peace or quiet of any neighborhood or person
By loud or unusual noise, tumultuous or offensive conduct, threatening, traducing, quarreling, challenging to fight, or fighting
enhancements: Involving violence: potential assault/battery charges
Resisting officers called to the disturbance: additional charges
notes: Idaho uses 'Disturbing the Peace' (I.C. § 18-6409) rather than 'Disorderly Conduct.' It is a broad misdemeanor covering a range of disruptive behavior. Often used as a plea-down from more serious charges.

elements: Defendant maliciously and willfully disturbed the peace or quiet of any neighborhood or person
notes: Same statute as disorderly conduct in Idaho (I.C. § 18-6409). Idaho does not distinguish between 'disturbing the peace' and 'disorderly conduct' — they are the same offense.

elements: Defendant willfully resisted, delayed, or obstructed a public officer
In the discharge or attempt to discharge any duty of the officer's office
enhancements: Violence against officer: additional assault/battery charges — I.C. § 18-915
Causing injury to officer: felony
notes: Idaho's resisting arrest statute (I.C. § 18-705) is a misdemeanor. It covers resisting, delaying, or obstructing — not just physical resistance. The arrest being resisted must be lawful, but defendants resist unlawful arrests at their own risk. Verbal resistance alone is generally insufficient.

statute_title: Intimidating, Impeding, or Influencing Officers, Jurors, Witnesses
elements: Defendant willfully attempted to influence, intimidate, or impede
A juror, witness, or officer in the discharge of their duty
In any case pending in any court
enhancements: Threats of violence: additional charges
Conspiracy to obstruct: additional charges
notes: Idaho's obstruction statute (I.C. § 18-2604) specifically addresses interference with judicial proceedings. Broader obstruction may also be charged under I.C. § 18-705 (resisting/obstructing officers). Destruction of evidence is a separate offense.

penalty_max: 5 days (direct contempt); varies (indirect contempt, up to 5 years if felony-related)
elements: Defendant willfully disobeyed a lawful court order
Or was disrespectful or disruptive in court proceedings
Or failed to appear as required
enhancements: Repeated contempt: cumulative sanctions
Contempt involving violence: additional criminal charges
notes: Idaho's contempt statutes are in Title 7 (Special Proceedings). Direct contempt (in the presence of the judge) can be punished summarily. Indirect contempt (out of court, e.g., violating a court order) requires notice and hearing. Criminal contempt can carry jail time.

penalty_max: 5 days (direct contempt); up to 5 years (certain violations)
elements: Defendant willfully defied the authority of the court
Beyond the scope of civil contempt remedies
The contempt was criminal in nature (punishment, not coercion)
enhancements: Repeat violations: escalating sanctions
notes: Criminal contempt in Idaho is punitive rather than coercive. Distinguished from civil contempt, which aims to compel compliance. Criminal contempt requires proof beyond a reasonable doubt.

elements: Defendant appeared in a public place
While intoxicated to a degree that constituted a danger to themselves, others, or property
notes: Idaho does not have a statewide public intoxication statute. Most public intoxication enforcement occurs under local city ordinances. The Idaho Supreme Court has noted that public intoxication alone is not a crime under state law — there must be an additional element (disturbing the peace, endangerment, etc.). Often addressed through protective custody rather than criminal charges.

offense_class: Misdemeanor (if underlying charge is misdemeanor); Felony (if underlying charge is felony)
elements: Defendant was released on bail or own recognizance
Defendant was required to appear in court
Defendant willfully failed to appear as required
enhancements: Felony failure to appear: separate felony charge
Forfeiture of bail
notes: Failure to appear matches the severity of the underlying charge. If the underlying charge is a felony, failure to appear is also a felony. Bail forfeiture is a separate civil consequence. A bench warrant is issued upon failure to appear.

statute_title: Providing False Information to Law Enforcement
elements: Defendant knowingly gave false information to a law enforcement officer or government agency
Concerning the commission of an offense
Knowing that the offense did not occur or that defendant had no information relating to the offense
enhancements: False report leading to arrest of another: potential additional charges
Filing a false police report: same statute
notes: Idaho's false report statute (I.C. § 18-5413) covers providing false information to law enforcement, state/local government agencies, and certain licensed professionals (social workers, psychologists, counselors). A misdemeanor offense.

offense_class: Misdemeanor (verbal threat without weapon); Felony (with deadly weapon or force likely to cause great harm)
elements: Defendant made an intentional, unlawful threat by word or act
To do violence to another person
Coupled with an apparent ability to carry out the threat
Creating a well-founded fear in the other person
enhancements: Use of a deadly weapon: aggravated assault (felony)
Threat directed at school: additional charges
notes: Idaho does not have a standalone 'criminal threats' statute. Threats are prosecuted under assault (I.C. § 18-901), which includes threats to do violence coupled with apparent ability. If a deadly weapon is involved, it becomes aggravated assault (I.C. § 18-905).

penalty_max: Original maximum sentence for the underlying offense
elements: Defendant was placed on probation for a criminal offense
Defendant violated one or more conditions of probation
The violation was willful or the defendant is unable to comply
enhancements: New criminal offense: substantive violation
Repeat violations: less discretion for continued probation
notes: Idaho courts have broad discretion in handling probation violations. The court may revoke probation and impose the original suspended sentence, modify conditions, or continue probation. A probation violation hearing uses a preponderance of evidence standard, not beyond a reasonable doubt.

elements: Defendant violated a non-criminal condition of probation
Such as missed appointment, failed drug test, missed curfew, failed to complete required program
enhancements: Pattern of technical violations: may lead to revocation
notes: Technical violations are non-criminal breaches of probation conditions. Idaho courts often use graduated sanctions (additional conditions, brief jail time, more restrictive probation) before full revocation. The Idaho Department of Correction uses evidence-based practices for technical violations.

offense_class: Same as underlying offense plus new offense
penalty_max: Original maximum sentence plus penalties for new offense
elements: Defendant committed a new criminal offense while on probation
The new offense constitutes a violation of probation conditions
enhancements: Violent new offense: strong presumption of revocation
New felony while on felony probation: likely revocation
notes: A substantive probation violation (committing a new crime) is treated more seriously than a technical violation. Courts are more likely to revoke probation and impose the original suspended sentence. The new offense is prosecuted separately.

elements: Defendant was released on parole
Defendant violated one or more conditions of parole
enhancements: New criminal offense: separate prosecution plus revocation
Absconding supervision: enhanced response
notes: The Idaho Commission of Pardons and Parole handles parole decisions. Parole violations may result in return to incarceration for the remainder of the sentence. Idaho uses a progressive sanctions model for technical parole violations.

offense_class: Same as underlying offense (felony conspiracy is a felony; misdemeanor conspiracy is a misdemeanor)
penalty_max: Same as the underlying target offense
fine_max: Same as the underlying target offense
elements: Defendant agreed with one or more persons to commit a crime
At least one overt act was committed by any member of the conspiracy in furtherance of the agreement
enhancements: Multiple co-conspirators: enhanced scope of liability
Conspiracy to commit violent crime: aggravating factor
