notes: Idaho's conspiracy statute (I.C. § 18-1701) requires an agreement plus an overt act. A conspiracy to commit a felony is a felony; conspiracy to commit a misdemeanor is a misdemeanor. Each conspirator is liable for foreseeable acts of co-conspirators committed in furtherance of the conspiracy.

elements: Defendant willfully made a false statement
Under oath or affirmation
In a proceeding where the oath or affirmation was required by law
The statement was material to the proceeding
enhancements: Perjury causing conviction of another: aggravating factor
Multiple instances of perjury: cumulative charges
notes: Perjury in Idaho is a felony punishable by up to 14 years — one of the more severely punished non-violent offenses. The false statement must be material to the proceeding. Subornation of perjury (inducing another to commit perjury) carries the same penalty.

elements: Defendant gave, offered, or promised something of value
To a public officer or employee
With corrupt intent to influence the officer's official act, vote, or decision
enhancements: Public official accepting bribe: same penalty
Pattern of bribery: additional charges
notes: Idaho's bribery statute (I.C. § 18-1301) covers both the giving and receiving of bribes. Punishable by up to 10 years in state prison. Covers executive, legislative, and judicial officials. The official forfeits their office upon conviction.

elements: Defendant willfully attempted to influence, intimidate, or impede a witness
In connection with any case or proceeding
Through threats, force, or corrupt persuasion
enhancements: Use of force or threats of violence: additional assault charges
Conspiracy to tamper: additional charges
notes: Witness tampering is prosecuted under I.C. § 18-2604 (intimidating witnesses) and I.C. § 18-2605 (bribing witnesses). Both are felonies. Includes preventing testimony, altering testimony, or retaliating against witnesses.

elements: Defendant willfully attempted to influence, intimidate, or impede a juror
In connection with any pending case
Through improper communication, threats, or bribes
enhancements: Use of force or threats: additional charges
Conspiracy: additional charges
notes: Jury tampering falls under the same statute as witness tampering (I.C. § 18-2604). Any attempt to influence a juror through improper means is a felony. Includes contact with jurors during trial and post-verdict intimidation.

elements: Defendant was lawfully confined in a prison, jail, or other correctional facility
Or was in the lawful custody of an officer
Defendant escaped or attempted to escape from such confinement or custody
enhancements: Use of force or violence during escape: additional charges
Escape from prison: runs consecutive to existing sentence
notes: Under I.C. § 18-2505, escape or attempt to escape is a felony carrying up to 5 years in addition to the existing sentence. Sentences for escape run consecutive to (not concurrent with) the sentence being served at the time of escape.

elements: Defendant falsely assumed or pretended to be a public officer
And acted in such pretended capacity
Or performed any act in such pretended capacity
enhancements: Impersonation to commit another crime: additional charges for underlying offense
notes: Idaho's impersonation statute (I.C. § 18-7007) covers impersonation of any public officer, not just law enforcement. It is a misdemeanor. If the impersonation is used to facilitate another crime (such as robbery or sexual assault), the underlying crime is charged separately.

elements: Defendant maliciously and with specific intent to intimidate or harass another person
Because of that person's race, color, religion, ancestry, or national origin
Committed or threatened physical harm, property damage, or harassment
enhancements: Bodily injury: aggravated charges
Pattern of harassment: enhanced sentencing
notes: Idaho's hate crime statute is called 'Malicious Harassment' (I.C. § 18-7902). It covers bias-motivated crimes based on race, color, religion, ancestry, or national origin. Notably does NOT include sexual orientation, gender identity, or disability as protected categories. Civil remedies are also available under I.C. § 18-7903.

penalty_max: 5 additional years on top of underlying offense
elements: Defendant committed a criminal offense
For the benefit of, at the direction of, or in association with a criminal gang
With the specific intent to promote, further, or assist criminal conduct by gang members
enhancements: Additional 5 years beyond the underlying offense sentence — I.C. § 18-8504
Recruiting juveniles into a gang: separate felony — I.C. § 18-8505
notes: The Idaho Criminal Gang Enforcement Act (I.C. § 18-8501 through 18-8510) provides sentence enhancements for gang-related crimes. It is an enhancement, not a standalone charge. The additional sentence runs consecutive to the underlying crime's sentence. Recruiting minors into gangs is a separate felony.

elements: Defendant intentionally and cruelly abused, mistreated, or neglected an animal
Or defendant tortured an animal
Or defendant intentionally or maliciously killed an animal
enhancements: Torture or intentional maiming: felony — I.C. § 25-3504
Repeat offense: felony
notes: Idaho's animal cruelty laws are under Title 25 (Animals). Basic cruelty is a misdemeanor. Torture, intentional maiming, or malicious killing of an animal is a felony. Exemptions exist for agricultural practices, hunting, and pest control.

statute_title: Bomb Threat / Threatening Use of Explosives
elements: Defendant threatened to place or detonate an explosive device
In a building, vehicle, or public place
With intent to cause fear or disruption
enhancements: Actual possession of explosive materials: additional charges
Threat against a school: federal prosecution potential
Resulting evacuation or injury: enhanced penalties
notes: Bomb threats are prosecuted as felonies in Idaho. Threats against schools, government buildings, and transportation infrastructure may also trigger federal prosecution. Even hoax threats carry serious penalties.

elements: Defendant used electronic communication to bully, harass, or intimidate another person
The conduct was repeated or severe
The conduct caused substantial emotional distress
enhancements: Threats of violence: potential felony assault charges
Targeting based on protected characteristics: malicious harassment — I.C. § 18-7902
notes: Idaho addressed cyberbullying primarily through school anti-bullying statutes (I.C. § 18-917A for student harassment). Criminal harassment and stalking statutes (I.C. § 18-7906, 18-7907) also apply to cyberbullying conduct.

elements: Defendant deposited waste, refuse, or materials on public or private property
Without authorization
In violation of environmental regulations
enhancements: Hazardous or toxic waste: felony charges
Environmental contamination: cleanup liability plus criminal penalties
notes: General littering and illegal dumping are misdemeanors under I.C. § 18-3904. Illegal disposal of hazardous waste elevates to a felony. Idaho's environmental statutes also impose civil cleanup liability separate from criminal penalties.

elements: Defendant recruited, harbored, transported, or obtained a person
Through force, fraud, or coercion (adult victim)
Or the victim was a minor (no force/fraud/coercion required)
For the purpose of labor or sexual servitude
enhancements: Minor victim: life imprisonment potential
Serious bodily injury: enhanced sentencing
Multiple victims: separate charges per victim
notes: Idaho enacted comprehensive human trafficking statutes in 2013 (I.C. § 18-8601 through 18-8605). Trafficking of a minor for sexual servitude does not require proof of force, fraud, or coercion. Victims have an affirmative defense to related prostitution charges. Idaho also provides for asset forfeiture in trafficking cases.

elements: Defendant was a public officer or employee
Defendant corruptly used their official position
To obtain personal benefit, accept bribes, or misuse public funds
enhancements: Embezzlement of public funds: I.C. § 18-5701
Pattern of corruption: aggregate charges
notes: Idaho addresses public corruption through multiple statutes: bribery (I.C. § 18-1301), embezzlement by public officers (I.C. § 18-5701), and official misconduct. Conviction results in forfeiture of office and permanent disqualification from holding public office.

elements: Defendant violated Idaho environmental protection statutes
Including illegal disposal of hazardous waste, water pollution, or air quality violations
The violation was knowing or negligent
enhancements: Knowing endangerment: enhanced penalties
Repeat violations: higher fines
Federal prosecution under RCRA, Clean Water Act, or Clean Air Act
notes: Idaho's environmental crimes are primarily under Title 39 (Health and Safety). The Idaho Department of Environmental Quality investigates violations. Significant cases are often referred to the EPA for federal prosecution.

elements: Defendant reasonably believed they were in imminent danger of great bodily harm or death
Defendant used no more force than reasonably necessary to defend against the threat
Defendant was not the initial aggressor
notes: Idaho is a Stand Your Ground state (I.C. § 19-202A) — there is no duty to retreat before using force in self-defense. Idaho also has Castle Doctrine provisions. Justifiable homicide is defined in I.C. § 18-4009 (defense of person) and I.C. § 18-4010 (defense of habitation). The burden shifts to the prosecution to disprove self-defense beyond a reasonable doubt once raised.

elements: Defendant aided, abetted, counseled, or encouraged another person to commit a crime
Defendant acted with the intent to promote or assist in the commission of the crime
The crime was committed
enhancements: All enhancements applicable to the principal offense
notes: Under I.C. § 18-204, all persons who aid and abet in the commission of a crime are treated as principals. They face the same penalties as the person who directly committed the offense. No distinction between principal and accessory before the fact in Idaho.

offense_class: Same as the underlying offense (reduced maximum for some crimes)
penalty_max: Life imprisonment (attempt of crime punishable by death or life); 5 years or half the maximum term for other crimes
elements: Defendant had the specific intent to commit a crime
Defendant took a direct but ineffectual act toward committing the crime
The act went beyond mere preparation
enhancements: Attempt of a capital crime: up to life imprisonment
notes: Under I.C. § 18-306, attempt carries up to life imprisonment if the target crime is punishable by death or life. For other crimes, the maximum is 5 years or half the maximum of the target crime, whichever is greater. Specific intent must be proven — recklessness or negligence is insufficient for attempt.

elements: Defendant remained in a public place with no apparent lawful purpose
Under circumstances that warrant alarm for the safety of persons or property
notes: Idaho does not have a statewide loitering statute. Loitering enforcement occurs under local city ordinances. Many loitering ordinances have been challenged on constitutional grounds (vagueness). Enforcement varies significantly by jurisdiction.

elements: Defendant produced noise exceeding local noise level regulations
During hours prohibited by local ordinance
notes: Idaho does not have a statewide noise ordinance. Noise violations are enforced under city and county ordinances. Excessive noise may also be prosecuted as disturbing the peace under I.C. § 18-6409 if it rises to that level.

offense_class: Misdemeanor; Felony (if causing significant bodily harm or involving sexual conduct)
elements: Defendant subjected another person to physical or psychological abuse
As part of initiation into or membership in an organization
Consent of the victim is not a defense
enhancements: Significant bodily injury: felony
Forced sexual conduct: felony plus sex offense charges
Death resulting: potential manslaughter charges
notes: Idaho's anti-hazing statute (I.C. § 18-917) covers any act of hazing regardless of the victim's consent. Organizations and individuals can be prosecuted. Schools and universities may impose additional administrative sanctions.

elements: Defendant was under court-ordered supervision
Defendant violated the terms of supervision
notes: Idaho does not use the term 'community control.' The equivalent is probation or community supervision, handled under the same probation violation statutes. Withheld judgments and suspended sentences may be revoked upon violation.

elements: Defendant made material misrepresentations in a mortgage loan application
Or defendant forged documents in connection with a mortgage transaction
With intent to defraud
enhancements: Multiple transactions: aggregate charges
Federal prosecution under 18 USC 1014
notes: Idaho does not have a standalone mortgage fraud statute. Mortgage fraud is prosecuted under general theft by deception (I.C. § 18-2403) and forgery (I.C. § 18-3601) statutes. Most significant mortgage fraud cases are prosecuted federally.

elements: Elements vary by specific offense
notes: Idaho criminal offenses not specifically categorized. Default penalties: misdemeanor maximum 6 months jail and $1,000 fine (I.C. § 18-113); felony maximum 5 years prison and $50,000 fine (I.C. § 18-112) when no specific penalty is prescribed.
